The "Export report" button freezes the dashboard: clicks on other buttons are ignored, and the "Preparing…" label shows up only after the report is ready. Last sprint, a developer "made it async": the number-crunching function now returns a promise and the click handler awaits it. The freeze is exactly as long as before, and the team is puzzled, because
calls in the same handler never froze anything.
The belief: if CPU-heavy work is wrapped in a Promise or an
function, it runs in the background, and the page stays responsive until the result comes back.
Smart developers believe this because async code really did fix their other freezes.
returns a promise and the page keeps scrolling while the request is in flight. In C#,

look the same in both languages. So "promise" quietly becomes shorthand for "runs somewhere else". The half-truth: the waiting in
happens outside JavaScript. Your loop is JavaScript, and it has nowhere else to run.
A promise is a receipt, not a thread
A promise is an object that stands for a result you'll get later. It says nothing about where the work happens. MDN's page on the

constructor is explicit: the executor is called synchronously, as soon as the promise is constructed. A loop inside the executor runs right there, on the caller's thread, before the constructor even returns.
async functions run synchronously until the first await
keyword doesn't change that. MDN puts it plainly: the code of an async function, up to and including the first
, runs synchronously, and an async function without an
runs synchronously from start to finish. What
gives you is a promise as the return value and the ability to pause at an
. Pausing only helps while you wait for something else; while your loop is computing, nothing is paused.
Why fetch doesn't block but your loop does

The browser performs the network request itself, outside your JavaScript. Your code starts it, gets a promise and returns. When the response arrives, the browser settles the promise and your callbacks run on the
. MDN describes it as the single thread where, by default, the browser runs all of your page's JavaScript, processes user events and paints. So while your loop runs, clicks and painting wait for it.

How to apply it in your project

items.title: Find CPU work hiding behind async

content.text: Look for loops, parsing, sorting, hashing or image processing inside
functions. If nothing inside awaits real I/O, the wrapper changes nothing about blocking.

items.title: Move pure computation to a worker

content.text: Work that takes data in and returns data, with no DOM access, fits a worker well. Wrap the

items.title: Slice what must stay on the main thread

content.text: If the work needs the DOM, split it into small chunks and yield with a task between them, so clicks and paints can run in the gaps.
